title: Rehras close
hook: morning Japji, evening Rehras: the day is held at both ends

segments.voice: Yesterday, sangat; your line was end the day together. Today, on our sixteenth day with Rehras, we close it.

Look at a shelf of books. Take away one bookend, and the row starts to lean. Take away both, and the books slide into a heap. Put a bookend back on each side, and the whole row stands up straight, even the thin ones in the middle. Nothing in the middle has changed. It's just held at both ends. That's the shape of the Sikh daily prayers.
screen: `A SHELF OF BOOKS.` → `NO BOOKENDS: THE ROW SLIDES.` → `HELD AT BOTH ENDS, IT STANDS.`

segments.voice: Sikhs call the daily prayers nitnem, the daily rule. In the morning, the Japji of Guru Nanak and the other morning banis. In the evening, Rehras. And at night, as we'll see tomorrow, Kirtan Sohila. Two bookends and a nightlight. Look back at what we packed for the road. Rehras opened at the door: so dar, what is that door, where everything sings. Hearsay calls You great; only one who has seen can say. Saying it I live, forgetting I die. So Purakh, that Being without stain. Kartaa, the river everything flows in. The pool of fire and water, feet stuck in the mud, and a hand from those who remember. Maanukh: this human life, your chance. A humble plea, with the word rahraas hidden inside. Why worry, mind, when even the rock-creatures eat? The Tenth Guru's Chaupai: shelter for the night. The Anand's joy, and a plate of truth, contentment and contemplation. Ardas, standing, asking that all be well. Dusk itself, sandhiaa. And the prayer said together. So what is Rehras for? The morning Japji sends a person out into the day. Rehras gathers them back in, with the same Name and many of the same Gurus. The hours in the middle, the commute, the meetings, the dishes, stand up straight because they're held from both sides.
screen: `NITNEM: THE DAILY RULE.` · `THE DOOR, HEARSAY, REMEMBERING, SO PURAKH.` · `THE MUD, YOUR CHANCE, THE PLEA, WHY WORRY.` · `CHAUPAI, ANAND, ARDAS, DUSK, TOGETHER.` · then, large: `BOTH ENDS HELD.`

segments.voice: Think back to this morning: was there a beginning, a line, a breath, a moment before the phone? If not, that's fine. Now choose tonight's bookend, a line of Rehras, the first line of the Chaupai, the Anand's joy has come, or a minute of quiet, and if you pray, say Waheguru once, for both ends.
Nitnem, the daily rule: sixteen days with the Sikh evening prayer, nine shabads, the Chaupai, the Anand, the Mundavani and Ardas, holding the day's far end as the Japji holds its start.
Your line: both ends held. However small the bookends, the middle stands. Tomorrow, the night song.

howItsDone: Sikh nitnem frames the day: the Japji and other banis in the morning, Rehras Sahib in the evening when work is done, and Kirtan Sohila at night before sleep.

fork.setup: a friend asks why Sikhs pray in the evening if they already prayed in the morning. what would you say?
options: the morning prayer wears off by noon.
the morning sends you out; the evening gathers you back: the day is held at both ends.
it's a penalty for a bad day.
fork.reveal: Japji at dawn and Rehras at dusk are bookends: the hours in the middle stand up straight because they're held from both sides.

original.note: Gurmukhi: nitnem, the daily rule; the set prayers that frame the Sikh day, morning, evening and night.

trapdoor: what you thought: Rehras is just the evening version of morning prayers.
what it means: its own prayer, packed for the road, that gathers the day back in as the Japji sent it out.

what a scholar hears: Rehras gathers five Gurus' voices, Guru Nanak, Guru Amar Das, Guru Ram Das, Guru Arjan and Guru Gobind Singh, and ends with passages that come at the close of the Guru Granth Sahib.

chat.says: You already prayed this morning. Why pray again in the evening and at night?
options: It's nitnem: Japji sends you into the day, Rehras gathers you back, Sohila closes the night.
The morning prayer wears off by evening, so it has to be topped up to keep working.
Evening prayer is only for days that went badly, to make up for what went wrong.
chat.meaning: Sikh nitnem holds the day at both ends: the Japji in the morning, Rehras in the evening, Kirtan Sohila at night.
